newsitem.title: USA: Mexican vote not likely to alter relations with US.
newsitem.headline: Mexican vote not likely to alter relations with US.

text.p: Mexico's landmark election results could ruffle the diplomatic surface in dealings with the United States, but analysts in and out of government said on Monday there were powerful incentives to get along.

Mexico's ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) appeared likely -- although not certain -- to lose its 68-year grip on the lower house of Congress when all of Sunday's results are in and was trounced in the first race this century for the symbolically important post of Mexico City mayor.
The prospect of dealing with a divided government in Mexico did not seem to faze Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who commented while in Madrid for a NATO summit.

"It is our custom that we respect the votes of the people in countries where they elect their legislatures or their presidents," Albright told a news conference. "We also have quite a lot of experience in dealing with countries where there is divided government, including our own."

President Bill Clinton appeared to hedge his bets when he visited Mexico in May, meeting separately with opposition leaders as well as with members of the PRI. He was hailed then as a "good friend of Mexico" by President Ernesto Zedillo, who reminded an enthusiastic audience of Clinton's support for the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) and for a $13.5 billion U.S. bailout of Mexico from financial crisis in 1995.

As the final returns were counted, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns congratulated Mexico for holding free and fair elections, saying this was an "important step in the advancement and consolidation of Mexico's democracy."

He amplified Albright's remarks on dealing with divided governments: "There's no reason that a democracy cannot survive with co-habitation. In fact, that really is the life-blood of a democracy, that certain parts of the government can be controlled by one party, others by another."

One U.S. official said there was unlikely to be any change in the U.S. stance on such knotty bilateral issues as drugs, immigration, the environment or trade as a consequence of the elections. But the official, speaking anonymously, acknowledged that a divided government might make relations "A more pluralistic and open society is something that we certainly applaud," the official said. "At the same time it makes governing a more complicated and difficult process, but that's a tradeoff which we certainly would welcome at any time."

George Grayson, an expert on Mexico at the College of William and Mary in Williamsburg, Virginia, said Mexico's leaders including Zedillo might indulge in more confrontational rhetoric, but substantively the U.S.-Mexico relationship would not change.

"Invariably there are white caps on the surface of U.S.-Mexican relations ... and there are likely to be more now that you've got the opposition increasing its presence in Congress and in Mexico City," Grayson said in a telephone interview from the Mexican capital.
"But well beneath the surface there are these strong, compelling currents that are just driving the two economies toward each other and integrating the two economies," he said.

One prevailing current is the rapid rise in bilateral trade, said Delal Baer of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Washington. She said trade between the two countries shot up in the last decade from $39 billion to $150 billion.

After years of dealing with a one-party system where approval by Mexico's Congress was not a primary concern, Baer said, a divided government would call for more patience on the part of the United States but need not lead to instability.

"A transition to democracy in Mexico does not automatically mean less stability," she said by telephone. "It could be noisy for a while and it will introduce more uncertainty into the environment but that doesn't necessarily mean instability."
Baer said the PRI and the conservative National Action Party (PAN) together retain enough seats in Congress to keep Mexico's economic reform policies on track.

Even before the votes were tallied, she was confident this course would continue: "I personally believe that it would be very difficult to turn the clock back on economic reforms in Mexico, no matter who wins."
